title: Electric or hybrid car: the 12 V battery, motors and wiring (leave the orange)
summary: Electric and hybrid cars still have an ordinary 12 V system: a battery, about eight small motors for windows, wipers and seats, lights, relays and wiring. All of that comes out with basic hand tools in about two hours. The big battery pack, the traction motor, the inverter and every orange cable can kill; this guide leaves them on the car.

steps.text: Pick the car. Choose one that has not been in a crash, fire or flood, with no hissing, no smell of burnt plastic or sweet chemicals, and no fluid dripping underneath. Work outdoors or in a big open space, away from buildings and other vehicles.
steps.warn: A crashed, flooded or burnt traction pack can catch fire hours or days later and its smoke is toxic. Leave that car alone and keep well clear of it.

steps.text: Make sure the car is fully off: no dashboard lights, no 'ready' sign. Take the key fob well away from the car (keyless cars can wake up when it is close). Put the parking brake on and chock a wheel. Open the hood and look around before you reach in.
steps.warn: A hybrid's petrol engine can start by itself while the car is 'ready'. Keep your hands out of the engine bay until the 12 V battery is disconnected.

steps.text: Learn what you must not touch. Orange cables, orange connectors and covers with a lightning-bolt label are the high-voltage system. They run from the big battery pack (under the floor or the rear seat) to the traction motor, the inverter, the air-conditioning compressor and the cabin heater. Walk around the car, look under the hood and find them all now. Everything orange stays on the car.
steps.warn: Don't touch, cut, unplug or open anything orange, even with the car off. A traction pack of several hundred volts can kill in an instant.

steps.text: Find the 12 V battery. It is in the trunk, under the hood, under a rear seat or behind a panel: the owner's manual or the fuse-box lid shows where. Most are lead-acid or AGM; some newer cars have a small lithium one. The label must say 12 V. Wrap your wrench handle in tape, take off the negative (-) clamp first, then the positive (+), tape both clamps and lift the battery out upright by its handles (see safety_lead_acid).
steps.warn: Never let a metal tool touch the positive terminal and the car body at the same time. A 12 V battery can weld a wrench to the bodywork.

steps.text: Leave every airbag, seat-belt pretensioner, the steering wheel and the steering column where they are. Don't unplug yellow connectors under the seats or in the doors, and leave alone any door card or seat marked SRS or AIRBAG. Wait at least 30 minutes after the 12 V battery is out before you work inside the cabin.
steps.warn: An airbag is an explosive charge. A disturbed module can fire hard enough to break bones, even with the battery out.

steps.text: Take the 12 V motors. Each is held by 2-4 bolts and one plug: window motors and door-lock actuators (remove the door card: screws behind the handle and in the armrest, then pry round the edge), the wiper motor and its linkage (under the cowl below the windscreen), mirror motors, the blower fan and any cooling fans that run on 12 V. Seat motors only from seats with no yellow airbag plug. Press the latch to unplug; never pull on the wires. Keep each motor's gear head and plug.

Take the lights and electrics: headlight and tail-light units (many are LED), interior lights, the horn, relays, fuses and the fuse boxes. Take 12 V wiring in lengths: cut about 15 cm each side of the plugs so you keep the connectors. Check every bundle before you cut: it must hold only thin wires.
steps.warn: Never cut an orange cable, a shielded cable, or any thick cable you can't trace back to the 12 V battery. If you can't tell, leave it.

steps.text: Take cabin parts that come out with a screwdriver or by unclipping: floor mats, carpet, sound-deadening mats, door speakers, rear seat cushion foam and covers, headliner fabric, sun visors. Leave anything with airbag markings.

Test the motors before you carry them away. From your 12 V battery, run a fused lead (10 A) to each motor's two terminals for a second. A good motor spins smoothly and reverses when you swap the leads. Window and wiper motors usually draw 2-8 A. Label each one.

Leave the traction pack, traction motor, inverter, charger, air-conditioning compressor, cabin heater and every orange cable on the car. The one exception: a pack that is already out of a car, standing on the ground or a pallet, with its case sealed and undamaged, dry, no cable cut or loose, and its connector covers in place. That can be moved whole with lifting gear and several people to a spot outdoors away from buildings. Never open it, cut it, unplug it, short it or bring it indoors. If any of that is not true, leave it.
steps.warn: Even with the car off and the 12 V battery out, the pack inside its case sits at hundreds of volts. Opening it can kill you, and the fire that follows will not go out with water.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **12 V battery.** Runs lights, a radio, a 12 V fridge or a phone charger. In a car that has sat for years it is often flat or sulfated: test it (test_lead_acid, test_lithium_cell). Small lithium 12 V batteries in newer cars are handled like any lithium pack (safety_swollen_lithium).
- **Window, wiper and seat motors.** Permanent-magnet 12 V DC motors with worm or planetary gears. Slow, strong and self-holding: good for a small winch (build_motor_winch), a door or gate opener, a solar tracker or a vent. Window motors draw several amps.
- **Fans.** 12 V blower and cooling fans: forge blowers, ventilation, cooling.
- **Lights.** LED headlights and tail lights run on 12 V and make good work lights.
- **Wiring, relays and fuses.** Ready-made 12 V harnesses with plugs; see skill_dc_wiring.
- **Charging cable.** Many EVs carry a mains charging cord in the trunk. If it is undamaged, its plug and heavy cable make a strong mains extension lead. Never open the control box on the cable.

## What stays on the car, and why

- **Traction pack.** 200-800 V DC, from a few kWh to over 100 kWh. Stays live when the car is off, and a 'service disconnect' does not make the cells inside safe. Taking it out takes training, insulated gloves and tools, and lifting gear: such packs weigh 250-600 kg. If a trained electrician or EV mechanic lives near you, tell them where the car is. A good pack can run a house for days.
- **Traction motor.** A permanent-magnet motor makes voltage when its shaft turns, so even rolling the car can energise its cables. Strong magnets too.
- **Inverter, charger and DC-DC converter.** Large capacitors that stay charged for minutes or longer. The DC-DC converter is what charges the 12 V battery while the car runs; you don't need it.
- **Air-conditioning compressor and cabin heater.** Both run from the high-voltage system and have orange cables. The compressor also holds refrigerant (safety_refrigerant).

## Hybrids and mild hybrids

- Full and plug-in hybrids have a 150-400 V pack as well as a 12 V battery: the same rules apply, and the petrol engine can start without warning. Treat the fuel as in safety_fuel_handling.
- Mild hybrids with a 48 V system are less deadly but carry heavy current. Leave the 48 V parts unless you are sure what they are.

## What to leave

- Anything orange, anything marked HV, and anything that smells or looks burnt.
- Crashed, flooded or burnt cars: the pack can ignite later.
